newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Albright sees Japan, Asia nations help to N. Korea.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees Japan, Asia nations help to N. Korea.

text.p: With crucial North Korea peace talks days away, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Tuesday she expected Japan to provide new food aid to Pyongyang and for Asian countries to help fund a landmark nuclear deal.

Foreign ministers at a regional meeting this week gave no specific commitment on her appeal for millions of dollars in funds to help underwrite the 1994 nuclear deal with North Korea, U.S. officials said.

But Albright told reporters she expected "more support for KEDO (Korean Energy Development Organisation) financially than previously ... I thought there was quite a lot of receptivity (at ASEAN) but we'll see if the check's in the mail".

North Korea was a major topic of discussion at ASEAN and the result was a greater understanding of KEDO's financial difficulties and how support for this body is integral to stability on the Korean peninsula, she said.
"People really focused a lot on the fact that the major strategic disruption that could come from the region could come from Korea, so there was a lot of focus on it," she added.
KEDO is the organisation that oversees North Korea's commitment to dismantle its nuclear programme.
On food aid, which the U.N. food programme says North Korea desperately needs to combat famine, Albright replied "yes" when asked whether Japan is now open to extending assistance to Pyongyang.

She attributed this to Pyongyang's recent announcement that Japanese women who moved to North Korea in 1959-60 -- and have not been heard from since -- may return home. This issue has been a major stumbling block between the two countries.

Albright held talks with Japan's foreign minister at the ASEAN meeting where Albright pressed members to contribute more to a $4.5 billion deal that has halted Pyongyang's nuclear programme for nearly three years.
The State Department refused to specify the exact amount of the U.S. request, saying it would be easier for ASEAN countries to give it serious consideration if the total was kept secret.
But it said Albright asked ASEAN to make a one-time contribution in the range of $10 million and then provide smaller contributions on an annual basis thereafter.
Washington believes Southeast Asian countries with some of the world's fastest-growing economies can afford the request, especially as the atomic deal helps ensure their security.
Albright's predecessor Warren Christopher made a similar request at last year's ASEAN meeting, but officials said this year's appeal was more aggressive and more direct.

It comes little more than a week before the Stalinist North is due to attend in New York on August 5 a preparatory meeting for peace talks aimed at replacing the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace treaty.
In addition to North Korea, the United States, South Korea and China are expected to attend. Albright said she feels North Korea and South Korea are ready to engage in a dialogue.

Japan and South Korea have pledged billions of dollars, and the United States $82.2 million, towards the 1994 accord, under which Washington vowed to provide $4.5 billion in new nuclear power plants and alternative energy supplies in return for North Korea freezing its nuclear programme.
At the time of the deal, the U.S. believed Pyongyang had enough capability and fuel to make one or two atomic bombs.
The U.S. plan was to set a target for ASEAN and let the countries decide themselves how to apportion the burden.
Although the United States negotiated the landmark deal with Pyongyang and is the moving force behind KEDO, Congress has been reluctant to appropriate the U.S. share.
President Bill Clinton has vowed to provide up to $25 million annually for the heavy fuel aimed at meeting North Korea's needs until the two new nuclear power plants are on line.
South Korean barges carrying trucks, bulldozers and heavy equipment left Seoul this week to begin building the plants.
